summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework governs what a trans visitor meets at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a visitor arriving on United States documents carries an identification that does not match their presentation at entry.

Airport screening follows federal procedure. Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and lead to secondary screening and pat-downs; travellers may request alternative screening and may decline the scanner. The agency's know-your-rights guidance extends to United States nationals travelling to and from the territory on the same terms as mainland travellers, including what may and may not be carried in hand baggage under the federal screening framework.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

Territorial law adds a layer of protection. The U.S. Virgin Islands human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending that protection explicitly into the education setting.

Relationship status is settled. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later federal recognition settled the question nationwide, so a married couple can rely on their marriage in the territory. The historic sodomy statute, applicable to the territory since 1957, has been replaced and is no longer in force.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting from July 2017 on the LGBTQ community in the U.S. Virgin Islands describes setbacks alongside reasons for hope, indicating a contested local climate rather than a settled one; the account does not set out a discrete trans-specific legal finding.

The territory's position as a United States territory means federal screening, document and funding rules operate alongside territorial anti-discrimination law, so a visitor may face restrictive national rules on entry and care while holding statutory protection against discrimination once inside the jurisdiction.

The Attorney General's 2017 interpretation is an official reading of existing anti-discrimination law rather than a new statute, which makes its scope in practice beyond the education setting a matter for enforcement rather than text.
localsOnly:
Residents of the U.S. Virgin Islands are covered by the territorial human-rights statute, which prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and by the March 2017 Attorney General interpretation holding that the law applies to transgender students in schools.

Same-sex marriage has been available in the territory since the 2015 Superior Court ruling, and marriages performed in the territory are federally recognised.

The historic sodomy statute applied to the territory from 1957 has been replaced and is no longer in force.

Federal know-your-rights guidance on airport security applies to residents on mainland routes on the same terms as other United States nationals, covering scanner refusal, alternative screening, and hand-baggage restrictions under the federal framework.

The January 2025 federal funding restriction on gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, which bears on residents' care access as well as visitors'.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement record of the territorial human-rights statute is not sourced here: no complaint outcomes, case law, or penalty figures for discrimination on gender-identity grounds are established by the inventory.

Whether the anti-discrimination statute's protections extend beyond education to public accommodations, housing, or restroom access in the territory is unresolved in the available sources.

The territory's current statute replacing the 1957 sodomy provision, and its text, are not specified in the inventory; only the fact of replacement is sourced.

Hate-crime provisions covering gender identity in the territory are not sourced, and no territory-specific violence data against trans people appears in the inventory.

The July 2017 reporting on setbacks and prospects for the LGBTQ community does not yield a discrete trans-specific legal claim and is left as context rather than a finding.
